text: Better a dry crust with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife.
A prudent servant will rule over a disgraceful son and share the inheritance among the brothers.
The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests hearts.
An evildoer listens to wicked lips; a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue.
Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; whoever gloats over disaster will not go unpunished.
Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and parents are the pride of their children.
Fine speech is not fitting for a fool—how much less are lying lips for a ruler.
A bribe is a magic stone in the eyes of the one who gives it; wherever he turns, he succeeds.
Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but whoever repeats a matter separates close friends.
A rebuke cuts deeper into a discerning person than a hundred blows into a fool.
An evil man seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger will be sent against him.
Better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly.
If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house.
Starting a quarrel is like breaching a dam; drop the dispute before it breaks out.
Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent—the LORD detests them both.
What good is money in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, when he has no sense?
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A person without sense strikes hands in a pledge and puts up security for his neighbor.
Whoever loves transgression loves strife; whoever builds a high gate invites ruin.

versions.text: Whoever loves strife loves transgression; whoever builds a high gate invites ruin.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "one who loves transgression loves strife" (אֹהֵב פֶּשַׁע אֹהֵב מַצָּה). The current rendering reverses subject and object, making strife the root and transgression the result, which inverts the proverb's logic.

text: A twisted heart finds no good, and one whose tongue is deceitful falls into trouble.

versions.text: A twisted heart finds no good, and a deceitful tongue falls into trouble.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew subject is a person ("the one perverse in his tongue"), not the tongue itself; as written, a tongue is said to fall into trouble, which is awkward when read aloud and shifts the parallelism away from the person.

text: Whoever fathers a fool does so to his grief; the father of a scoundrel has no joy.
A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.
The wicked accepts a bribe in secret to pervert the ways of justice.
Wisdom is right there before the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth.
A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to the mother who bore him.
It is not good to fine the innocent, or to flog honorable men for their integrity.
Whoever restrains his words has knowledge, and a person of understanding keeps a cool spirit.
Even a fool who keeps silent is thought wise; if he holds his tongue, he seems discerning.
